To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the numbers of unobscured and obscured AGNs are similar at 8 μm, and that the numbers of quasars and Seyfert 1 nuclei are similar at 24 μm.

the fraction of AGN with MIR luminosities comparable to quasaries and that are missed because of dust obscuring their optical emission is ~ 40% and that the fraction of obscured and unobsured AGNs is comparable in samples selected in MIR at S(8) ~ 1mJy.
the numbers of unobscured and obscured quasars in the FLS are similar at S_(8) ~ 1mJy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the selection of AGNs in MIR surveys.
the selection of AGNs in the MIR, the discovery of obscured quasars, the identification of quasars in the SDSS, and the properties of the FLS sample of 16 likely obscured AGNs.
the identification and study of obscured AGNs in the MIR.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are ~16 objects that are probably obscured quasars in the FLS, and that the numbers of unobscured and obscured AGNs at S_(8) ~ 1mJy are comparable.
the fraction of AGN that are missed in the SDSS because of extinction in our MIR selected sample is ~50%.
the fraction of obscured AGNs is ~50% at S_(8) ~ 1.0 mJy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fraction of luminous AGNs that are obscured by dust is ~ 50% in samples selected at MIR fluxes of 1 mJY.
the fraction of AGN candidates that are obscured by dust is ~50% at MIR luminosities comparable to quasar luminosities.
the fraction of luminous AGNs obscured at 8 μm by dust is ~ 30%.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the MIR is an excellent wavelength for selecting obscured AGNs, as well as unobscured ones, because it is less affected than the optical by obscuration and reddening.
the FLS has a large number of objects that have colors that are indicative of AGN activity, and that the FLS will be a rich source of obscured AGNs.
the MIR is a good wavelength regime to identify AGNs, and that the MIR luminosity of the AGN is a useful indicator of the degree of extinction of the optical continuum.
